Strategic: Borda's honest men are rare, and a theorem says why it matters. Allan Gibbard in 1973 and Mark Satterthwaite in 1975 proved independently that with three or more options, every rule that picks a winner and is not a dictatorship can be manipulated: there is always some situation in which some voter does better by voting against their true ranking. It is Arrow's theorem seen from the voter's side. Part seventeen's deferred acceptance made honesty safe for one side only because matching is not a vote over one outcome that everyone shares.

Agora checked every way each group of like-minded islanders could change its ballot. Under plurality, the 11 fruit-first islanders, seeing the fruit trail the fish, can all vote for the boat race instead, their second choice; the boat race wins, which they prefer to the fish. That is voting for the lesser evil. Under Borda's count, the 12 fish-first islanders can push the boat race, the leader, to the bottom of their ballots; the market fair, their second choice, wins instead. That is called burying. Under instant runoff, the same 12 can put the market fair first; it survives the early rounds and wins, which they much prefer to the dance. Only the market fair, the Condorcet winner, cannot be beaten this way: a plan that wins every head-to-head vote leaves no group a better deal.

Called it? In 1951 the French political scientist Maurice Duverger argued that plurality voting in single-member districts tends to produce two parties, because voters desert third parties that cannot win, and politicians stop joining them: strategic voting, on a national scale. In the United States, every president since 1853 has been a Democrat or a Republican. But Britain, Canada and India, which also elect by plurality, keep third and regional parties in parliament, strong where their voters are concentrated. Partly right: a tendency within each district, rather than a law for the nation.
Welfare: Chapter seven. Welfare functions: Bentham, Rawls and Atkinson.

To go further, a welfare function must say how to weigh people against each other. Here are five islanders' incomes, from five baskets a week to eighty. Jeremy Bentham's answer was to add up everyone's happiness. If happiness rose in step with income, only the total would matter, and this island would score its mean, thirty-one, however the baskets were shared. John Rawls's answer, for the basic structure of a society, was to judge it by how its worst-off member fares. Then only the minimum, five, counts. Between them lies a family. Let each person's utility grow ever more slowly as income rises, at a rate set by one number, epsilon. At epsilon zero this is Bentham with income; at epsilon one, utility is the logarithm of income; and as epsilon grows without limit, the sum behaves like Rawls's minimum.

Anthony Atkinson, in 1970, turned the family into a measure. Ask: what income, if everyone had the same, would this welfare function value exactly as highly as the island's real incomes? He called it the equally distributed equivalent. At epsilon zero it is the mean, thirty-one. Now raise epsilon. At one it is twenty, the geometric mean; at two, about thirteen; and it sinks toward the minimum, five. One minus its ratio to the mean is Atkinson's index of inequality. At epsilon one it is nought point three five: a society that cared this much about equality would give up thirty-five percent of its income, if the rest could be shared equally, and count itself no worse off.

Arthur Okun gave epsilon a picture in 1975: a leaky bucket. Carry one basket from the richest islander, with eighty, to the poorest, with five. Taxes and administration make the bucket leak. How much may leak before the transfer makes society worse off? At epsilon zero, none: a basket is a basket. At epsilon a half, 75 percent of it may leak. At epsilon one, 94 percent. At epsilon two, almost all of it. Atkinson's lesson was that every measure of inequality, the Gini coefficient included, holds a judgment like this one, whether or not it says so. His made it a number you have to choose.
CBA: Chapter ten. Cost-benefit analysis as applied social choice.

Cost-benefit analysis is social choice done with money. The island considers a new jetty. Ana, the richest, would pay up to thirty baskets for it; Friday, the poorest, would lose ten baskets' worth of fishing ground. The usual analysis adds the money: thirty minus ten is twenty, so build it. That is Kaldor and Hicks's test, in money. But willingness to pay depends on what you have. A basket means more to someone with five than to someone with eighty. Weight each person's money by Atkinson's rule: mean income over their own, raised to epsilon. At epsilon a half, the jetty's net value turns negative, minus 6.2. At epsilon one, it is minus 50: don't build it. The case for leaving the weights out, made by Louis Kaplow and Steven Shavell, is that taxes redistribute more cheaply than distorted projects do, so projects should be judged on efficiency alone. Its force depends on whether the taxes really follow.

This is where the measuring stops and a judgment begins. Economics can measure the jetty: thirty baskets' worth for Ana, ten lost by Friday, twenty gained in all. Whether to build it needs a judgment about how much a basket to Friday counts against a basket to Ana, which is epsilon, and about whether Friday will in fact be compensated. An analysis that uses no weights has still made a choice: epsilon zero.

The same judgment reaches across time. Gains in a century must be set against costs today, and the tool is the discount rate. Frank Ramsey's formula from 1928 splits it into two parts: delta, pure impatience, and eta times g, where g is growth and eta is the epsilon of this part, now saying how much less an extra dollar means to a richer future. Nicholas Stern's review of climate change in 2006 set delta near zero, at nought point one percent, eta at one and growth at one point three percent: a rate of one point four percent. At that rate, a million dollars a hundred years away is worth about 249 thousand today. At three percent, about 52 thousand. At four and a half percent, near the market returns that William Nordhaus argued for, about 12 thousand. A factor of twenty, from the rate alone. Delta and eta are ethical choices, not facts waiting to be measured. Part forty-eight puts them to work on the climate.
Capabilities: Chapter twelve. Capabilities: what to measure.

Everything so far has added up incomes or utilities. Sen asked whether either is the right thing to add. Income is only a means. What it buys depends on your health, where you live, whether you have a disability, and what the law lets you do. And happiness adapts: people who have little often learn to want little, so a measure of satisfaction can make deprivation look acceptable. Sen proposed judging a society by people's capabilities: what they are able to do and to be. To live a long life, to read, to move freely, to take part in the life of the community. Which capabilities count, and how to weigh them, is a question for philosophy; Part thirty-eight of Philosophy, Built takes it up.

The data show why it matters. Each dot is a country in 2023: income per head across, on a log scale, and life expectancy up. Richer countries live longer, but the spread at any income is wide. Sri Lanka and Equatorial Guinea have almost the same income, a little under thirteen thousand dollars a head. Sri Lankans live to about seventy-seven and a half; Equatorial Guineans to about sixty-four: fourteen years apart. Cuba, with an income about a ninth of America's, has almost the same life expectancy, and Costa Rica, with less than a third, a longer one. Qatar, one of the richest countries, has long lives too. Income is a poor guide to the capability that matters most: staying alive.

In 1990 the Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq, working with Sen, turned the idea into a number for the United Nations. The Human Development Index combines health, education and income. Each part is scaled from nought to one between a floor and a goal, income entering as a logarithm, and since 2010 the three have been combined by a geometric mean. It reorders the world. Qatar ranks 4th by income, but 43rd by the index. Cuba ranks 127th by income and 97th by the index; the United States 10th and 18th. But its weights are a choice too. Martin Ravallion showed in 2012 that in the poorest countries, the index treats a year of life as worth very little income. Every index is a welfare function in disguise. Ask what it trades for what.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the value of a statistical life.

Here is the dial, every value converted to 2024 dollars. Ashenfelter and Greenstone's speed limits give an upper bound of about three million dollars, with wide uncertainty. The Environmental Protection Agency's central value, from a distribution fitted to twenty-six studies, mostly of wages and risks, is seven point four million in 2006 dollars, about 11.5 million today. And the Department of Transportation uses 13.7 million for analyses in 2024. The status: contested. The number moves by more than a factor of four with the method and with whose choices are observed. It returns in part fifty-eight, where a bill is scored.

Why such a spread? Wage studies compare risky jobs with safe ones, but risky jobs differ in more than risk, the omitted variables of part four. The people in risky jobs may also care less about risk; they chose those jobs. People misjudge small probabilities, so what they accept may not be what they would choose if they understood the risk. And the speed-limit study values time at the wage, which makes it an upper bound by design. A regulator still needs one number, and choosing it is part of the policy.
